processing: Anhua raw dark tea, steamed and packed into a bamboo, leaf and smartweed wrapping, then squeezed by twisting, stomping, rolling and hammering. The Qian Liang size then dries in the open air for 49 days.
harvest_season: Sold by size and pressing year rather than by picking. One seller's lots are listed as spring tea.
appearance_dry: A long cylinder wrapped in patterned bamboo, with tight dark tea inside; sizes run from a small ten-tael roll to a column about 160 cm tall.
appearance_liquor: Clear orange-yellow when young, moving to orange-red with age.
taste_profile: A pine-led aroma with a thick, mellow body. One aged Shi Liang lot is described as spicy, sweet and thick, with hints of yeast and mushroom.

brewing.notes: Remove the bamboo and saw off discs or break off chips. Rinse once and use boiling water.

vintage_note: Sold whole by size and pressing year, often aged, and cut into slices or samples by some shops. Size matters as much as year: the name covers ten, hundred and thousand-tael rolls. Ask for the maker, year and actual weight.
description:
Hua Juan, the flower roll, is the one roll in Anhua's three tips, three bricks and one roll. Today it usually goes by the name Anhua Qian Liang and includes ten, hundred, thousand and even larger tael sizes. The flower is the pattern left on the tea by its woven wrap.

Making one is a team job. Steamed raw dark tea goes into a bamboo, leaf and smartweed casing, and workers twist, stomp, roll and hammer it tight. The big column is about 160 cm tall and 20 cm across, weighing about 36 kg, and dries outdoors for 49 days.

In the cup you get a pine scent and a thick, soft body. Aged rolls grow sweeter and more complex. The tea is very hard, so a saw beats a knife, and small chips brew more evenly than thick chunks.

When buying, the family name tells you little, so check size, maker and year. Baishaxi is the factory most linked to its modern revival. A smaller Shi Liang roll is the sensible first buy.
history:
Hunan press accounts date Qian Liang, the largest roll, to the Jiaqing to Daoguang years, when workers packed loose dark tea tightly so it would carry better by mule. A separate English account credits Shanxi merchants in the Tongzhi years. A roll discovered in the Palace Museum in 1983, first mistaken for pu-erh, was later traced to Anhua and dated to about 1796 to 1820.

The Baishaxi factory, founded in 1939, played a leading part in reviving the craft, and Qian Liang-making became national intangible heritage in 2008.
